fields.h1: Build a History Quiz That Shows Which Questions Stump People
fields.hero_description: Build a history quiz on any era, with sourced answers and scoring, and see which questions your class or team missed.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a History Quiz
fields.features_subheading: Emergent writes the questions, serves them one screen at a time, and saves every answer to a table you own.
fields.feature_1:
Questions from the period you name

Name the fall of Rome, the Civil War, or the 1960s, and Emergent drafts multiple-choice questions whose wrong options come from the same period. Edit any of them before sharing.
fields.feature_2:
A table of every answer

Each response is saved with the player's name, the question, and whether it was right, in a database you own. Sort the table by question to see which one stumped the whole room.
fields.feature_3:
One question per screen

Players move through the quiz one question at a time, a flow that fits a phone held in one hand at a trivia table or beside an exhibit. A QR code on a slide or placard opens it.
fields.feature_4:
The why behind each answer

After a player answers, the app shows a short explanation with the source you chose for it, and a wrong guess teaches the date or the treaty instead of just costing a point.
fields.feature_5:
A recap when the quiz closes

Set a closing time, and the app emails the host a recap with the average score, each player's total, and the most-missed questions. Alerts can also go to Slack or stay in the app.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain, your code

The quiz can live at your own domain; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. Paid plans export the full code to your GitHub repository for a developer to extend.

fields.tab_content_1:
The 14th Amendment question comes back before the test

Westbrook High's two US History sections, 54 students in all, close the Reconstruction unit with a 15-question review quiz. Each answer is saved with student and section. Question 11, on the 14th Amendment, was missed by 31 of 54, more than any other, and Thursday's warm-up goes back to it before the unit test.
fields.tab_content_2:
One question stumped 12 of the 14 teams

At Tuesday trivia, The Copper Lantern runs a 10-question world history round, with 14 teams answering on their phones, one question per screen. Answers land under each team's name. The Hanseatic League question was missed by 12 of the 14 teams, and Current Events took the round with 9 of 10.
fields.tab_content_3:
The flood panels get rewritten after 240 answers

Marlow County Historical Society put a QR code beside its courthouse exhibit that opens a 12-question local history quiz. 240 visitors took it in October. The 2 questions on the 1936 flood scored lowest, 91 and 98 right of the 240, and the curator rewrites those panels first.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every episode ends in a 10-question quiz

Each episode of The Longview History Podcast ends with a 10-question quiz linked from the newsletter. 412 listeners took the Suez Crisis quiz, and a recap in the show's Slack named the most-missed question: the canal's nationalization, missed by 287 of the 412. The next episode opens with it.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a History Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to make a history quiz with checkable questions, sourced answers, and a table that shows what to reteach.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick one period and one audience
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Wrong options from the same era
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Put a source under every answer
fields.howto_step_1_des: Name the stretch of history the quiz covers, such as Reconstruction or the Cold War, and who takes it: a class, trivia teams, or newsletter readers. Put both in the prompt so the questions come out pitched at that group.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Favor dates, names, places, and outcomes, where one option is right, and the rest are plainly wrong. Skip questions that invite debate, such as what caused a war, and save those for the discussion after the scores come in.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Wrong options should name people or events of the same kind from the same period: four presidents, four treaties, four battles. An option from the wrong century gives the answer away and teaches nothing when it is ruled out.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Under each question, add one line that states the answer and names where it comes from, such as an archive, a museum, or a primary document. Shown on the result screen, that line settles a disputed answer at the table.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write the result bands before launch: what 9 of 10 says about the player, and what 4 of 10 suggests reviewing. Check that every possible score lands in exactly one band before anyone plays.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Ask 2 people from the real audience to take the quiz on a phone before it goes out. Rewrite any question the two of them read differently, and confirm their answers landed in the table under the right names.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Sort the table by question after the first run and take the hardest one back to the next class, round, or episode. Ask it again a month later and compare the two runs to see whether the reteach worked.
fields.hero_prompt: Build a history quiz on Reconstruction for my two US History sections that scores each student and lists the most-missed questions.

faq_plan.a: A history quiz is a set of questions about past events, people, and places, each with one checkable answer, scored at the end. Classrooms run one to review a unit, trivia nights build themed rounds from one, and museums and podcasts use one to learn what their visitors or listeners already know.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a history quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe the quiz in one sentence to Emergent's AI survey builder: the period it covers, who takes it, and how many questions it asks. Emergent builds the quiz with scoring and a results table, and you share it as a link or a QR code. One prompt changes a question, a band, or the look.

faq_plan.q: How many history quiz questions should one round have?
faq_plan.a: Ten history quiz questions fit a trivia round or a newsletter quiz, and a class review carries 15 to 20 so every topic in the unit appears at least once. Keep a phone round short enough to finish in about 5 minutes, and cut questions rather than let the back half rush.

faq_plan.q: Can I reuse my history quiz questions and answers for other subjects?
faq_plan.a: Yes: the format carries over whole. The one-right-answer structure, the bands, and the results table work the same whether the questions cover treaties or rivers. A geography quiz reuses the build with new questions; keep one app per subject so each table stays easy to read.

faq_plan.q: What changes in a history quiz for kids?
faq_plan.a: Keep the questions shorter, the options fewer, and the names familiar. A history quiz for kids works better with 3 options instead of 4, and with result messages that name what a kid got right rather than what they missed. Read each question aloud once, and split any that takes two breaths.

faq_plan.q: Can I build a free history quiz without a paid plan?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Emergent is free to start, and the free tier covers building and publishing a page with a live URL. Response caps do not apply either: surveys and quizzes take unlimited responses, whether 20 students answer or 240 visitors scan the exhibit code.

faq_plan.q: Can one history quiz app host a different round each week?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The questions live in the app's own database, and editing them is a prompt, not a rebuild, while past rounds keep their scores in the table under their date. Rotate themes the same way, from a world history round to a bible quiz, without touching the scoring or the bands.

faq_plan.q: How do I stop players searching answers during a history quiz?
faq_plan.a: Give each question a timer: 20 seconds pulls answers from memory, while 2 minutes leaves room for a search bar. Emergent builds the flow one question per screen, which keeps the next question hidden while the clock runs. Shuffle the option order between players as well, and nobody gains by glancing at a neighbor.

faq_plan.q: What should players see when they finish a history quiz?
faq_plan.a: Show the score, the band message, and the question list with each right answer, its explanation, and its source. Players argue less when the source sits next to the answer. Keep the host view separate: the table of answers by player and question belongs on your dashboard, not on the player's screen.

faq_plan.q: How often should the questions in a history quiz change?
faq_plan.a: Swap them as soon as the same players return: a weekly history round needs fresh questions every week, while a class can rerun the same 15 after a month to measure the reteach. Word drills age differently; a vocabulary quiz can repeat sooner, because practicing the same words is the point.

plan.angle: The top 10 is all quizzes to take, not to run: Britannica, BuzzFeed, Sporcle, HistoryColored and ushistoryquiz.com host their own trivia, Mentimeter offers a fixed template, and the AI Overview generates a throwaway 5-question round inline. None shows how to run a history quiz as your own app, with your own questions and a table of who missed what. This page gives the searcher both: an 8-question history quiz to play on the page with every answer sourced, then four history quizzes a teacher, a bar, a historical society and a podcast run as their own app, each saving answers to a table sorted by question.
